sections.label: The opening
sections.line: Precedent, as in English law, settles cases nobody predicted
sections.para: A business will never write down every variation of its decisions. English law's answer fits agents: principles from the top, unsettled cases decided by a person and recorded, matching cases following that precedent, differing ones distinguished and escalated. Precedents that hold become policy, then code, given a decision record good enough to be a law report.

sections.label: In short
sections.line: Distinguished cases escalate; precedents that hold become code
sections.para: Nobody can predict every case, so statutes set principles, courts decide cases and precedent carries answers forward; for agents, envelopes come from the top and unsettled cases escalate. A case whose facts differ in a way that matters goes to a person. What keeps holding becomes policy, then code, which needs a record, not a log.

sections.label: The cases nobody predicted
sections.line: Envelopes catch far-out cases but not the ordinary ones
sections.para: Approving at altitude makes extreme cases visible but leaves the ordinary ones inside every envelope and covered by no rule: a late but intact order's refund, a memory deletion by a non-owner, a release with a borderline failing test. A policy listing every case becomes a contract nobody reads; it needs a way to settle and learn.

sections.label: How English law does it
sections.line: English law binds by precedent, distinguishes and can overrule
sections.para: Statutes set principles, read by purpose, even via Hansard under Pepper v Hart. Delegated rules beyond their powers are ultra vires, like the tribunal fees order quashed in 2017. Higher courts bind lower ones, differing cases are distinguished, and since the 1966 Practice Statement the top court can depart from its own decisions.

sections.label: The same shape for agents
sections.line: Each legal element has an equivalent in agent decisions
sections.para: An Act maps to the principles and envelope, delegated legislation to lower-altitude policies, a court to a person deciding an escalated case, a judgment to the decision record. A case is settled by a rule, else by a matching precedent, else it goes to a person whose recorded decision becomes the next precedent.

sections.label: How a decision earns its way into code
sections.line: Cases move a decision from a person into code
sections.para: Case law moves a decision up the scale: a person decides with context and records why, precedent settles the matching cases afterwards, the policy absorbs a rule that has held, and finally code enforces it as a test, CI check, tool limit or gate. Each step is earned by real cases, not assumed in advance.

sections.label: What a decision record needs
sections.line: A precedent needs facts, rule, decider, outcome and reasons
sections.para: A log is not enough: a precedent records the facts the decision turned on, the policy and altitude it was decided under, who decided with what authority, the outcome and the reasons. Without these a system cannot distinguish a case. In the SGit × Ruflo run, every policy decision is computed and none written down.

sections.label: Two small cases from tonight
sections.line: One evening set a rule and distinguished a case
sections.para: A figure shipped with an unchecked date, so the precedent is that a figure's facts are checked like the body's; one case sufficed under "verify every fact". Two commits without a leak scan were in throwaway test repositories that never published, so the case was distinguished and the counter should count only covered repositories.

sections.label: Where the analogy stops
sections.line: Agent precedent is fast, can spread bias, lacks opposition
sections.para: Legal precedent takes years and two sides; an agent's can be set in a minute by one person. A wrong decision followed a thousand times is a thousand wrong decisions, so overruling matters more. Nobody argues the other side, and judging material facts is itself a decision a person should make at first.

sections.label: The series
sections.line: Third of four: policies, altitude, case law, mapping
sections.para: The series has four parts: Three policies for an agent, on behaviour, decision and workflow; Approve at altitude, narrow, never widen; this piece, Case law for agents; and Three decisions, mapped. That last part works through the scenarios element by element.

sections.label: What this does not claim
sections.line: A proposal borrowing law's shape, not legal advice
sections.para: It is not legal advice or a summary of English law, only the shape of precedent taken from introductory sources. No agent system I know keeps decision records as precedents; the loop is untested, and the two cases are small. Lawyers who find the analogy wrong can write to agent@riskmandate.ai.
